lead: Fabrication is a sequence of masks. Each mask lets one layer be grown, deposited, implanted or cut in a fixed order. Temperature decides what can come after what, and alignment decides how the layers land on each other. Follow an nMOS transistor first, then the extra masks that put an nMOS and a pMOS on the same die. The order explains why source and drain are self-aligned to the gate, and why contacts and metal come last.
prereq: You need: the chapter on oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation for oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation, and the chapter on lithography, etching and deposition for lithography, etching and deposition; the MOS structure and its operating regions for what a transistor needs.

blocks.text: Begin with a p-type silicon wafer. The active mask defines the islands where transistors will sit. Outside each island the field oxide, a thick oxide, isolates neighbours.

items: Form field oxide outside the active islands. LOCOS, local oxidation of silicon, grows thick oxide locally but spreads sideways as a bird's beak. STI, shallow trench isolation, etches a trench and fills it with oxide.
Grow the gate oxide, a thin SiO<sub>2</sub> layer, then deposit polycrystalline silicon (poly).
Use the poly mask and etch to leave the gate. Dope the poly so it conducts.
Implant a light n<sup>−</sup> dose for the lightly doped drain, LDD. The poly gate and field oxide block the implant elsewhere.
Deposit an oxide spacer and etch it back. The spacer sets the offset for the heavy n<sup>+</sup> implant.
Implant n<sup>+</sup> source and drain, then anneal to activate dopants. The poly gate with its spacers is the mask, so source and drain line up with the gate without a separate alignment.
Open contacts, deposit and pattern metal, passivate, and open the pads.

blocks.text: The self-aligned step is the key. If source and drain were implanted through a separate window, mask misalignment would leave a gap or overlap. With the gate as the mask, the only offset comes from the spacer, set by deposition and etch, not by lithography.

sections.h3: The CMOS flow: wells and two S/D masks

blocks.text: CMOS, complementary MOS, needs an nMOS and a pMOS. In a simple n-well flow on a p-type wafer, the pMOS sits inside an n-well. The n-well mask comes before the active mask: implant phosphorus and drive it in. The nMOS stays in the p-substrate. Well variants are in the chapter on p-well, n-well and twin-tub processes.

After wells, the flow repeats the nMOS steps: active, gate oxide, poly, poly mask. Then it splits. The n+ source/drain mask covers the pMOS area with resist and opens the nMOS area. An arsenic or phosphorus implant makes n+ source and drain. The p+ source/drain mask covers the nMOS and opens the pMOS. A boron implant makes p+ source and drain. Two masks exist because one implant must not enter the other transistor: n+ in a p+ region would compensate the doping.

Then come contact, metal 1, via (a hole etched in the oxide between two metal layers and filled with metal), metal 2, and pad. Each is one lithography step with its own mask. The figure lists all ten masks in order. The back end starts at contact: wiring, not transistor formation.

The order follows temperature and alignment. Well implants and isolation see high-temperature drives, so they come before the gate oxide. The gate oxide must stay clean and thin; later high-temperature steps are limited. Poly is deposited after gate oxide, and the source/drain implant comes after poly because the poly is the mask. The activation anneal follows the implants. Contacts and metal come after that anneal because metal wiring cannot take the same heat.

The line splits into front-end-of-line (FEOL), where transistors are made, and back-end-of-line (BEOL), where contacts, vias and wires are made. Contact is the first back-end step. Passivation protects the chip; the pad mask opens windows over the pads so a bond wire or probe can touch metal.

MOS memory processes reuse this flow and add layers. DRAM adds a stacked capacitor; flash adds a floating gate. The cells and their operation are in Memory design: SRAM, DRAM and ROM. Here, only note that memory adds masks; it does not change the logic of the mask sequence.
The mask flow is the middle of a longer chain, and some syllabi ask for the whole wafer-to-chip flow. Each stage hands the next a product it can test.

items: Crystal growth: a single-crystal silicon ingot is pulled from molten silicon (the Czochralski method), doped p- or n-type.
Wafer preparation: the ingot is sliced into wafers, today 300 mm across and under 1 mm thick, then lapped, etched and polished to a mirror finish.
Front end: wells, isolation, gate and source/drain, as above.
Back end: contacts, vias and metal layers, then passivation and pad openings.
Wafer probe: every die is tested on the wafer and failing dies are marked.
Dicing: the wafer is sawn into separate dies.
Packaging: good dies are attached to a package, joined by bond wires or solder bumps, and sealed.
Final test: packaged chips are tested again, sorted by speed, and shipped.

blocks.text: N is the number of whole dies on a wafer of diameter d (cm) for die area A (cm²); the second term removes the part dies at the edge. Y is the fraction of dies with no killer defect when defects of density D (per cm²) fall at random.

spec.aria: Two rows of five boxes: n-well, active, poly, n+ and p+ source/drain masks, then contact, metal 1, via, metal 2 and pad masks, with the yield and good-die count.

examples.question: A CMOS process uses these masks, one lithography step each: n-well, active, poly, n+ source/drain, p+ source/drain, contact, metal 1, via, metal 2, pad. (a) How many lithography steps? (b) A die is 0.5 cm² and the line has D = 1 defect/cm²; use Y = e<sup>−A·D</sup> for yield. (c) How many steps if metal 2 is dropped? (d) How many good dies does a 300 mm wafer give? Use N ≈ π(d/2)²/A − πd/√(2A).
steps: Count the masks: n-well, active, poly, n+ S/D, p+ S/D, contact, metal 1, via, metal 2, pad. That is 10 masks, and one lithography step each gives 10 steps.
For yield, A = 0.5 cm² and D = 1 defect/cm². A·D = 0.5 × 1 = 0.5. Y = e<sup>−0.5</sup> = 0.6065. As a percentage, 60.7%, about 61%.
Drop metal 2. The via connects metal 1 to metal 2, so the via mask also goes. Steps = 10 − 2 = 8.
examples.answer: (a) 10 lithography steps; (b) Y = 0.607, about 61%; (c) 8 steps; (d) 1319 dies per wafer, of which about 800 work.
examples.check:
import math
n = 10
A = 0.5
D = 1.0
Y = math.exp(-A * D)
print(n)
print(round(Y, 3))
print(n - 2)

traps: Saying source and drain are diffused through a window. They are implanted with the poly gate acting as the mask; that self-alignment keeps gate and source/drain from drifting apart.
Mixing up mask count with layer count. A mask is one lithography step; one layer may use more than one mask, and one mask may open more than one hole.
Dropping metal 2 but keeping the via mask. The via connects metal 1 to metal 2, so both go together.
Merging the n<sup>+</sup> and p<sup>+</sup> source/drain masks. The same implant would counter-dope one transistor.
Putting contact before the source/drain anneal. Contact holes come after high-temperature steps.

quiz.q: Name the two isolation methods used between active islands.
quiz.a: LOCOS, local oxidation of silicon, and STI, shallow trench isolation.

quiz.q: Why is the source/drain implant called self-aligned?
quiz.a: The poly gate itself blocks the implant, so source and drain are placed by the gate edge; no separate alignment step is needed.

quiz.q: A CMOS flow uses n-well, active, poly, n+ S/D, p+ S/D, contact, metal 1, via, metal 2, pad. How many masks if only one metal layer is used?
Why must the n+ S/D mask cover the pMOS area?
quiz.a: It keeps the n+ implant out of the p+ source/drain. Otherwise the n+ donors would compensate the p+ acceptors and raise the pMOS source/drain resistance.

quiz.q: Why do wells come before gate oxide?
quiz.a: Well formation needs a long, hot drive-in. If the gate oxide were already there, that heat would thicken it, let impurities in and spread any channel doping, so the wells and isolation are made first and the gate oxide is grown after them.

quiz.q: A die is 0.8 cm² and D = 0.5 defects/cm². Use Y = e<sup>−A·D</sup>. Find Y.
Why is an oxide spacer formed before the heavy n+ implant?
quiz.a: The spacer offsets the heavy implant from the gate edge and leaves the lightly doped LDD region under the spacer. This reduces the peak field.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern lines replace LOCOS with STI and add high-k gate oxide with a metal gate. FinFETs move the channel into a fin, but the mask idea remains. Process engineers use TCAD simulation and a process design kit (PDK) to check each step before silicon. Search for 'CMOS process integration', 'STI', 'high-k metal gate' and 'TCAD process simulation'.
